purpose: Amiodarone is used to treat serious irregular heartbeats, such as ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia, that can be life-threatening. It helps your heart beat in a steady, normal rhythm. Doctors usually prescribe it when other heart rhythm medicines have not worked.
how_it_works: Your heart beats because of electrical signals that travel through it in a very organized way. When those signals go haywire, your heart can beat too fast, too slow, or in a chaotic pattern. Amiodarone works by slowing down those electrical signals and stabilizing the heart muscle so it can beat in a more regular, safe rhythm.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, feeling tired or dizzy, sensitivity to sunlight (skin can burn more easily), a bluish-gray skin discoloration with long-term use, blurred or altered vision, and abnormal thyroid lab results. Some people notice a metallic taste in their mouth.
warnings: Amiodarone is a powerful medicine with serious potential risks. It can damage your lungs, liver, and thyroid gland, so your doctor will monitor you with regular blood tests, chest X-rays, and eye exams. It can also cause new heart rhythm problems in rare cases. Tell your doctor about ALL other medications you take, as amiodarone interacts with many drugs including blood thinners like warfarin. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use sunscreen daily.
typical_dosing: Dosing is very individualized. A common starting dose for adults is 800 to 1600 mg per day in divided doses for the first 1 to 3 weeks, then reduced to 600 to 800 mg per day for about a month, and then a maintenance dose of 200 to 400 mg once daily. Your doctor will adjust your dose based on how your body responds and your lab results. Always take it exactly as prescribed.
